title: Example: Mixed Step 1 Systems
description: Five original Step 1-style questions across renal pharmacology, cardiology, microbiology, hematology and neurology. Use it to try tutor and exam modes.

questions.stem:
A 64-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy comes for follow-up. Three months ago, a medication was added to his regimen of carvedilol, lisinopril and furosemide because his left ventricular ejection fraction remained 30% despite therapy. He now reports **tender enlargement of both breasts**. His blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg.

| Serum | Value |
|---|---|
| Na⁺ | 137 mEq/L |
| K⁺ | 5.6 mEq/L |
| Creatinine | 1.2 mg/dL |

Which of the following medications was most likely added?

options.explanation: Digoxin can rarely cause gynecomastia (estrogen-like structure), but it does not cause hyperkalemia at therapeutic levels, and it improves symptoms without reducing mortality. Hyperkalemia occurs only in acute toxicity.

Eplerenone is a selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist. It also reduces mortality in HFrEF and can cause hyperkalemia, but it has minimal affinity for androgen and progesterone receptors, so gynecomastia is rare. It is the usual substitute when gynecomastia develops.

Correct. Spironolactone blocks aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct (lowering K⁺ excretion → hyperkalemia), and its non-selective antiandrogen and progesterone-receptor activity causes gynecomastia. It lowers mortality in HFrEF with EF ≤35%.
Thiazides cause hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia, and do not cause gynecomastia. They have no mortality benefit in HFrEF.
An ARNI can raise K⁺ (via angiotensin II receptor blockade), but it does not cause gynecomastia. It must not be combined with lisinopril (angioedema risk; needs a 36-hour washout).

questions.explanation: Both mineralocorticoid antagonists cause **hyperkalemia**, because blocking aldosterone in the principal cells of the collecting duct reduces ENaC activity and K⁺ secretion. Spironolactone also blocks androgen receptors and stimulates progesterone receptors, which shifts the estrogen-to-androgen balance in breast tissue and causes gynecomastia. Eplerenone is selective for the mineralocorticoid receptor, so switching to it keeps the mortality benefit in HFrEF while sparing the breast.
questions.discriminator: Mineralocorticoid antagonist + gynecomastia = spironolactone (non-selective, antiandrogenic); eplerenone is selective and spares the breast.

questions.stem:
A 71-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of palpitations and mild exertional dyspnea for 2 days. She has a history of COPD. Her pulse is 75/min and regular; blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg. A rhythm strip is shown.

Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this arrhythmia?

options.text: Macro-reentrant circuit in the right atrium that passes through the cavotricuspid isthmus
options.explanation: Correct. Typical atrial flutter is one large reentrant loop around the tricuspid annulus. It produces regular sawtooth flutter waves at about 300/min, and the AV node conducts every 2nd to 4th wave (here 4:1, giving 75/min). Ablating the isthmus is curative.

options.text: Multiple chaotic reentrant wavelets, often initiated by ectopic foci in the pulmonary veins
options.explanation: Atrial fibrillation has no discrete P or flutter waves and an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm. This strip shows organized, regular sawtooth waves.

options.text: Conduction over an accessory pathway that bypasses the AV node
options.explanation: Wolff-Parkinson-White shows a short PR interval and a delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke) in sinus rhythm. It does not produce continuous sawtooth atrial activity.

options.text: Enhanced automaticity of several atrial foci
options.explanation: Multifocal atrial tachycardia (common in COPD) shows at least 3 distinct P-wave morphologies with varying PR intervals and an irregular rhythm, not uniform sawtooth waves.

options.text: Triggered activity from early afterdepolarizations in the ventricles
options.explanation: Early afterdepolarizations underlie torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with twisting QRS amplitude in the setting of a prolonged QT.

questions.discriminator: Regular sawtooth waves at ~300/min with fixed AV block = flutter (organized macro-reentry); irregularly irregular with no P waves = fibrillation.
questions.source: Original question (qbank-player example); ECG is a schematic drawing

questions.stem:
A 23-year-old man comes to the physician because of 10 days of bloating, flatulence and greasy, foul-smelling stools that float. He returned from a week-long backpacking trip 2 weeks ago, during which he drank water from mountain streams that he treated with chlorine tablets. He has no fever and no blood in the stool. Abdominal examination shows mild diffuse tenderness.

Which of the following best describes the most likely causal organism?

options.text: Acid-fast oocysts that cause severe watery diarrhea mainly in immunocompromised patients
options.explanation: Cryptosporidium is also chlorine-resistant and waterborne, but it causes watery (not fatty) diarrhea. It is most severe in patients with low CD4 counts and is identified by acid-fast oocysts.

options.text: Trophozoites that ingest red blood cells and cause flask-shaped colonic ulcers
options.explanation: Entamoeba histolytica causes bloody dysentery and can cause liver abscesses. Malabsorption with steatorrhea is not typical.

options.text: Comma-shaped, oxidase-positive rods that produce a cAMP-raising toxin
options.explanation: Vibrio cholerae causes profuse "rice-water" secretory diarrhea, not steatorrhea, and is not associated with treated mountain stream water.

options.text: Flagellated protozoan whose cysts resist chlorination and whose trophozoites attach to the duodenal mucosa
options.explanation: Correct. Giardia lamblia cysts survive standard chlorination. Trophozoites attach to the duodenal and jejunal brush border with a ventral sucking disk, causing malabsorption with fatty, foul-smelling stools, bloating and flatulence without fever or blood. Treat with metronidazole or tinidazole.

options.text: Gram-negative rod that produces heat-labile and heat-stable enterotoxins
options.explanation: Enterotoxigenic E. coli (traveler's diarrhea) causes acute watery diarrhea that resolves within days. It does not cause prolonged steatorrhea.

questions.discriminator: Chlorine-resistant cysts + steatorrhea without blood or fever = Giardia; watery diarrhea in an immunocompromised host with acid-fast oocysts = Cryptosporidium.

questions.stem:
A 26-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of fatigue, back pain and dark urine for 2 days. Four days ago, he started trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection. His conjunctivae are icteric. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL, the reticulocyte count is 6%, haptoglobin is undetectable, and indirect bilirubin is elevated. The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is negative. A peripheral blood smear shows erythrocytes with pale, notch-like defects at the edge, and supravital staining shows dark intracellular inclusions.

Decreased production of which of the following molecules is most directly responsible for this patient's condition?

options.explanation: Low ATP is the defect in pyruvate kinase deficiency. That causes chronic extravascular hemolysis from early life without drug or oxidant triggers, and shows echinocytes (burr cells) rather than bite cells and Heinz bodies.

Correct. G6PD deficiency (X-linked) reduces NADPH production in the pentose phosphate pathway, so glutathione cannot be kept in its reduced state. Oxidant stress (sulfonamides, primaquine, dapsone, fava beans, infection) then denatures hemoglobin into Heinz bodies. Splenic macrophages remove them, leaving bite cells, and episodic hemolysis follows.
Spectrin and ankyrin defects cause hereditary spherocytosis: spherocytes, a positive EMA-binding or osmotic fragility test, and chronic hemolysis with splenomegaly. It is not triggered by drugs.

Loss of GPI anchors (PIGA mutation) causes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. CD55 and CD59 are missing, leading to complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis and thrombosis. It is not drug-triggered and has no Heinz bodies.
Reduced ALA synthesis (for example, B6 deficiency) causes sideroblastic anemia, a production defect with ringed sideroblasts and a low reticulocyte count, not acute hemolysis.

questions.discriminator: Oxidant trigger + Heinz bodies/bite cells + Coombs-negative = G6PD (NADPH); chronic untriggered hemolysis = PK deficiency (ATP) or spherocytosis (membrane).

questions.stem:
A 57-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 9-month history of progressive difficulty buttoning his shirt and climbing stairs, and, more recently, slurred speech and choking on liquids. Examination shows atrophy of the hand intrinsic muscles, **fasciculations of the tongue and thighs**, spasticity in the lower extremities, brisk reflexes, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Sensation is intact to all modalities. Eye movements and sphincter function are normal.

Which of the following drugs is most likely to modestly prolong survival in this patient?

options.explanation: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor for myasthenia gravis, which causes fatigable weakness, ptosis and diplopia. Reflexes are normal, and there are no fasciculations or upper motor neuron signs.
Used for Guillain-Barré syndrome and multifocal motor neuropathy. Both are lower-motor-neuron or peripheral processes with reduced reflexes, not hyperreflexia and Babinski signs.

A disease-modifying therapy for multiple sclerosis, which typically causes relapsing deficits including sensory and visual symptoms. Tongue fasciculations and muscle atrophy (lower motor neuron signs) do not fit.
Treats Parkinson disease, which causes bradykinesia, rigidity and resting tremor, without weakness, fasciculations or Babinski signs.

Correct. Combined upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski) and lower motor neuron signs (atrophy, fasciculations), with normal sensation, eye movements and sphincters, indicate amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Riluzole reduces presynaptic glutamate release (less excitotoxicity) and prolongs survival by a few months.

questions.discriminator: UMN + LMN signs with pure motor involvement (sensation, eye movements and sphincters spared) = ALS, treated with riluzole; LMN-only or sensory involvement points elsewhere.
